name: HERA
description: A unified taxonomy for identifying ethical and regulatory risks in mHealth applications (AI and non-AI).
sources: DTX Risk Assessment Canvas (Denecke et al., 2023)
WHO Ethics & Governance of AI for Health (2024)
Beauchamp & Childress — Four Principles of Biomedical Ethics

pillars.name: Patient Safety & Clinical Risk
pillars.description: Risks related to clinical harm, misdiagnosis, unsafe recommendations, and over-reliance on the app.

dimensions.name: Clinical Evidence & Validation
dimensions.description: Has the app's clinical effectiveness been validated through appropriate studies?
reflection_questions: What clinical evidence supports the effectiveness of your app?
Has your app been tested in a controlled clinical trial or pilot study?
Are the clinical guidelines your app relies on up-to-date and peer-reviewed?
example_risks: App provides health recommendations without clinical validation
Underlying clinical model is based on outdated guidelines
example_mitigations: Conduct a pilot study with target patient population
Establish a clinical advisory board to review content regularly

dimensions.name: Contraindications & Adverse Effects
dimensions.description: Could the app cause harm to specific patient groups or in certain conditions?
reflection_questions: Are there patient groups for whom your app could be harmful?
Have you identified situations where the app's recommendations could lead to adverse outcomes?
Does the app clearly warn users about conditions where it should not be used?
example_risks: App used by patients with comorbidities not accounted for in the algorithm
No warning for pregnant users when app recommendations may be unsafe
example_mitigations: Implement contraindication screening at onboarding
Display clear warnings for known risk groups

dimensions.name: False Sense of Security
dimensions.description: Could the app give users unwarranted confidence in their health status?
reflection_questions: Could a user interpret the app's output as a definitive diagnosis?
Does the app clearly state it does not replace professional medical advice?
What happens if the app fails to detect a serious condition?
example_risks: User assumes normal readings mean they are healthy and skips checkups
App provides reassuring messages that mask deteriorating conditions
example_mitigations: Add prominent disclaimers that the app is not a diagnostic tool
Recommend periodic professional checkups regardless of app results

dimensions.name: Delayed Medical Consultation
dimensions.description: Could the app cause users to postpone seeking professional medical care?
reflection_questions: Could your app lead users to self-manage conditions that require medical attention?
Does the app include triggers that recommend users consult a doctor?
What is the escalation path when the app detects concerning patterns?
example_risks: User relies on symptom tracker instead of visiting emergency care
App chat feature gives users the impression they are receiving medical care
example_mitigations: Implement red-flag alerts that urge immediate medical consultation
Set time-based reminders for professional follow-up

dimensions.name: Measurement Reliability
dimensions.description: Are the measurements and data captured by the app accurate and reliable?
reflection_questions: How accurate are the sensors or self-reported data your app relies on?
Have you validated measurement accuracy against clinical-grade instruments?
How does the app handle noisy, incomplete, or erroneous data?
example_risks: Smartphone sensor provides inaccurate heart rate readings
Self-reported symptom data is inconsistent or unreliable
example_mitigations: Cross-validate sensor data with certified medical devices
Implement plausibility checks on user-entered data

dimensions.name: System Dependency & Over-reliance
dimensions.description: Could users become overly dependent on the app for health management?
reflection_questions: Could long-term use of your app reduce the user's ability to manage their health independently?
Does the app encourage self-efficacy or create dependency?
What happens if the app becomes unavailable — can the user still manage?
example_risks: Patient stops monitoring symptoms without the app
Disruption in app service leads to missed medication doses
example_mitigations: Design the app to build user knowledge and autonomy over time
Provide offline backup instructions for essential functions

pillars.name: Data Ethics & Privacy
pillars.description: Risks related to the collection, storage, sharing, and governance of personal health data.

dimensions.name: Informed Consent
dimensions.description: Do users fully understand what data is collected and how it is used?
reflection_questions: Is your consent process written in plain language that patients can understand?
Do users know exactly what data is collected, why, and who has access?
Can users give granular consent (choosing which data types to share)?
example_risks: Consent form is too technical or legalistic for average users
Users agree to data collection without understanding the implications
example_mitigations: Use layered consent with a plain-language summary and detailed version
Implement visual consent flows with concrete examples

dimensions.name: Data Minimization
dimensions.description: Does the app collect only the data strictly necessary for its function?
reflection_questions: What data do you collect, and is every data point necessary for the app's core function?
Are there data fields you collect 'just in case' that could be removed?
Do you collect location, contacts, or device data beyond what's needed?
example_risks: App collects GPS data when only city-level location is needed
Health data is collected for analytics that don't benefit the user
example_mitigations: Audit every data field and justify its necessity
Implement data collection review as part of each release cycle

dimensions.name: Storage, Encryption & Security
dimensions.description: Is personal health data properly secured at rest and in transit?
reflection_questions: Where is user health data stored — on-device, cloud, or both?
Is data encrypted at rest and in transit (TLS 1.2+, AES-256)?
Who has access to the encryption keys and the stored data?
example_risks: Health data stored in plaintext on shared cloud infrastructure
API endpoints transmit sensitive data without encryption
example_mitigations: Implement end-to-end encryption for all health data
Conduct regular penetration testing and security audits

dimensions.name: Third-Party Data Sharing
dimensions.description: Is health data shared with third parties, and are users aware of this?
reflection_questions: Does the app share any user data with third parties (analytics, advertisers, researchers)?
Are users explicitly informed about every third-party data recipient?
What safeguards exist to prevent re-identification of shared data?
example_risks: Analytics SDK sends health data to third-party servers
Data shared with insurers could affect user's coverage or premiums
example_mitigations: Eliminate all non-essential third-party SDKs
Implement data processing agreements with all third parties

dimensions.name: Anonymization & Right to Erasure
dimensions.description: Can users have their data deleted, and is shared data properly anonymized?
reflection_questions: Can users request complete deletion of their data (GDPR Art. 17)?
Is data anonymized before being used for research or analytics?
Could anonymized datasets be re-identified through linkage attacks?
example_risks: User account deleted but data persists in backups and analytics
Small patient populations make anonymization ineffective
example_mitigations: Implement automated data deletion pipelines across all storage layers
Apply k-anonymity or differential privacy for small populations

dimensions.name: Vulnerable Population Data
dimensions.description: Are there special protections for data from children, elderly, or mental health patients?
reflection_questions: Does your app serve minors, elderly, or people with cognitive impairments?
Are there additional consent requirements for vulnerable populations?
How do you ensure that vulnerable users understand data implications?
example_risks: Children's health data collected without parental consent
Mental health data used without heightened protection
example_mitigations: Implement age-gating and parental consent flows
Apply stricter data handling policies for sensitive health categories

pillars.name: Patient Autonomy & Therapeutic Relationship
pillars.description: Risks related to patient decision-making, manipulation, and the impact on the doctor-patient relationship.

dimensions.name: Right to Make Decisions
dimensions.description: Does the app respect the patient's right to make their own health decisions?
reflection_questions: Does the app present options or does it prescribe a single course of action?
Can users override or ignore the app's recommendations?
Does the app support shared decision-making with healthcare providers?
example_risks: App pushes users toward specific treatments without presenting alternatives
Users feel pressured to follow app recommendations without question
example_mitigations: Present recommendations as options with pros/cons
Include 'discuss with your doctor' prompts for medical decisions

dimensions.name: Emotional Manipulation & Excessive Nudging
dimensions.description: Does the app use persuasive techniques that could undermine autonomous decision-making?
reflection_questions: Does your app use gamification, streaks, or rewards that could become compulsive?
Are push notifications designed to help the user or to drive engagement metrics?
Could the app's tone or messaging create anxiety or guilt?
example_risks: Streak-based design makes users feel guilty for missing health tasks
Fear-based notifications cause unnecessary anxiety
example_mitigations: Audit all nudging mechanisms for patient benefit vs. engagement metrics
Allow users to customize or disable notifications entirely

dimensions.name: Impact on Doctor-Patient Relationship
dimensions.description: Could the app weaken the relationship between patient and healthcare provider?
reflection_questions: Does the app position itself as a replacement for professional medical advice?
Can the app share data with the patient's healthcare provider?
Does the app encourage or discourage professional consultations?
example_risks: Users treat chatbot interactions as equivalent to doctor visits
Data from the app is not accessible to treating physicians
example_mitigations: Include explicit messaging that the app complements, not replaces, medical care
Provide data export features for sharing with healthcare providers

dimensions.name: Dynamic Consent & Withdrawal Rights
dimensions.description: Can users change their mind about participation and data sharing at any time?
reflection_questions: Can users withdraw consent for specific data uses without losing app functionality?
Is the withdrawal process as easy as the consent process?
Are users informed about what happens to their data after withdrawal?
example_risks: Withdrawing consent requires contacting support rather than a simple toggle
Core features are locked behind all-or-nothing data consent
example_mitigations: Implement in-app consent management dashboard
Design graceful feature degradation when specific consents are withdrawn

dimensions.name: Automation Bias (AI and Non-AI)
dimensions.description: Do users or clinicians over-trust the app's outputs, even when they are wrong?
reflection_questions: Could users accept the app's output without critical evaluation?
Does the app communicate uncertainty and confidence levels?
Have you tested what happens when the app gives incorrect recommendations?
example_risks: Clinician follows app's risk score without clinical judgment
Patient trusts app's 'all clear' and ignores worsening symptoms
example_mitigations: Display confidence intervals or uncertainty indicators
Require active user acknowledgment for critical recommendations

pillars.name: Quality, Usability & Technical Reliability
pillars.description: Risks related to app stability, usability, accessibility, and technical quality.

dimensions.name: App Stability & Error Handling
dimensions.description: Does the app handle failures gracefully without risking patient safety?
reflection_questions: What happens if the app crashes during a critical health measurement?
Are errors communicated clearly to the user with recovery instructions?
Is there a fallback mechanism for essential functions?
example_risks: App crash during medication reminder causes missed dose
Error messages are too technical for patients to understand
example_mitigations: Implement graceful degradation for critical features
Use patient-friendly error messages with clear next steps

dimensions.name: Interoperability & Data Exchange
dimensions.description: Can the app exchange data with other health systems (EHR, FHIR)?
reflection_questions: Does your app support standard health data formats (HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT)?
Can data be exported to or imported from electronic health records?
Does the app work with other health devices the patient might use?
example_risks: Health data locked in proprietary format, inaccessible to other providers
Incompatible data formats lead to transcription errors
example_mitigations: Implement FHIR-compliant data export
Test integration with major EHR systems in target markets

dimensions.name: Accessibility (WCAG, Literacy, Language)
dimensions.description: Is the app usable by people with disabilities, low literacy, or different languages?
reflection_questions: Does your app meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards?
Is the health information written at an appropriate literacy level?
Is the app available in the languages spoken by your target population?
example_risks: Visually impaired users cannot use the app with screen readers
Health instructions written at a reading level above target users
example_mitigations: Conduct accessibility audit against WCAG 2.1 AA
Test content readability at 6th-grade reading level

dimensions.name: User-Centered Design & Usability Testing
dimensions.description: Has the app been designed and tested with real end users?
reflection_questions: Have you conducted usability testing with representative users?
Were patients, caregivers, and clinicians involved in the design process?
How do you collect and act on user feedback after launch?
example_risks: App designed by engineers without patient input
Critical features are hard to find or confusing to use
example_mitigations: Conduct iterative usability testing with 5+ representative users per round
Establish a patient advisory panel for ongoing feedback

dimensions.name: Offline Functionality & Updates
dimensions.description: Does the app work without internet, and are updates managed safely?
reflection_questions: Can users access essential features without internet connectivity?
How are app updates deployed — do they interrupt critical functions?
What happens to user data during an update?
example_risks: Patient in rural area loses access to medication schedule without wifi
Forced update during health emergency disrupts app access
example_mitigations: Cache essential data locally for offline access
Allow users to defer non-critical updates

pillars.name: Transparency & Explainability
pillars.description: Risks related to opaque decision-making, unclear limitations, and lack of traceability.

dimensions.name: Understandable Output
dimensions.description: Can users understand how the app produces its results or recommendations?
reflection_questions: Can a typical user understand why the app gave a specific recommendation?
Is the logic behind scores, alerts, or risk levels explained?
If the app uses AI, is the user informed and can they understand the reasoning?
example_risks: App shows a risk score without explaining contributing factors
AI-generated recommendations appear as black-box outputs
example_mitigations: Provide plain-language explanations for every recommendation
Show contributing factors for scores and risk assessments

dimensions.name: Clear Communication of Limitations
dimensions.description: Does the app clearly communicate what it cannot do?
reflection_questions: Does the app clearly state its intended use and boundaries?
Are users warned about conditions or scenarios where the app is unreliable?
Is it clear that the app is not a medical device (if applicable)?
example_risks: Users assume the app covers conditions it was not designed for
Marketing overpromises relative to validated capabilities
example_mitigations: Display limitations prominently in onboarding and settings
Include scope statements in every health-related output

dimensions.name: Decision Traceability & Logging
dimensions.description: Can decisions and recommendations be traced back and audited?
reflection_questions: Are the app's recommendations logged for later review?
Can a clinician trace why the app gave a specific recommendation at a specific time?
Is there an audit trail for regulatory compliance?
example_risks: No record of what the app recommended when an adverse event occurred
Cannot demonstrate regulatory compliance during an audit
example_mitigations: Implement immutable logging of all health-related recommendations
Store versioned model/algorithm state alongside outputs

dimensions.name: Clinically Validated vs. Estimated Content
dimensions.description: Is it clear to users which content is evidence-based and which is generated or estimated?
reflection_questions: Does the app distinguish between clinically validated information and AI-generated content?
Are sources cited for health information?
Can users tell the difference between evidence-based and estimated outputs?
example_risks: AI-generated health text presented as if it were clinically validated
No source attribution for medical information
example_mitigations: Label all content with its evidence level
Cite clinical guidelines or studies where applicable

pillars.name: Equity, Bias & Social Justice
pillars.description: Risks related to unfair treatment, exclusion, and reinforcement of health inequalities.

dimensions.name: Data & Clinical Rule Bias
dimensions.description: Are the data or clinical rules underlying the app biased toward certain populations?
reflection_questions: Were the datasets used to build your app representative of your target population?
Are clinical thresholds or scoring rules validated across different demographics?
Have you tested for disparate outcomes across gender, age, and ethnicity?
example_risks: Dermatology app trained mostly on light skin tones misses conditions in darker skin
BMI-based recommendations do not account for ethnic variation in body composition
example_mitigations: Audit training data and clinical rules for demographic representation
Conduct subgroup analysis in validation studies

dimensions.name: Digital Divide & Socioeconomic Access
dimensions.description: Is the app accessible to users regardless of their socioeconomic status or digital literacy?
reflection_questions: Does the app require expensive hardware, high-speed internet, or advanced digital skills?
Is the app free or affordable for low-income users?
Have you considered users who share devices or have limited data plans?
example_risks: App requires latest smartphone, excluding lower-income users
Subscription model creates barrier for those who need it most
example_mitigations: Support older devices and low-bandwidth connections
Offer free tier for essential health features

dimensions.name: Cross-Cultural & Multilingual Validation
dimensions.description: Has the app been validated across cultures and languages?
reflection_questions: Has the app been tested with users from different cultural backgrounds?
Are health concepts and metaphors culturally appropriate?
Have translations been validated by native-speaking health professionals?
example_risks: Direct translation loses medical nuance
Cultural taboos around certain health topics not accounted for
example_mitigations: Use professional medical translators, not machine translation alone
Conduct cultural sensitivity review with local health experts

dimensions.name: Impact on Existing Health Inequalities
dimensions.description: Could the app widen the gap between those who have good health access and those who do not?
reflection_questions: Could your app disproportionately benefit already-advantaged populations?
Have you assessed whether the app could worsen existing health disparities?
Is the app designed to reach underserved communities?
example_risks: App adoption concentrated in urban, educated, tech-savvy populations
Digital health tool replaces in-person services in underserved areas without adequate support
example_mitigations: Partner with community health organizations for distribution
Monitor adoption metrics by demographic group

dimensions.name: Representativeness in Validation Studies
dimensions.description: Were the studies validating the app conducted with representative populations?
reflection_questions: Did your validation studies include participants from your actual target demographics?
Were minority groups, elderly, and low-literacy users included in testing?
Are your study results generalizable to the populations who will use the app?
example_risks: App validated only with university students, deployed to elderly patients
Clinical trial excludes non-English speakers who are part of target market
example_mitigations: Define inclusion criteria that match real-world target population
Report demographic breakdown in validation study results

pillars.name: Regulatory Compliance & Governance
pillars.description: Risks related to legal classification, regulatory conformity, and organizational governance.

dimensions.name: Medical Device Classification (SaMD)
dimensions.description: Is the app a Software as a Medical Device, and is it classified correctly?
reflection_questions: Does your app provide diagnosis, treatment recommendations, or clinical decision support?
Have you assessed whether your app qualifies as a medical device under MDR 2017/745?
What risk class would your app fall under (I, IIa, IIb, III)?
example_risks: App providing diagnostic guidance marketed as 'wellness' to avoid regulation
Incorrect classification leads to insufficient safety testing
example_mitigations: Conduct formal SaMD classification assessment with regulatory consultant
Document intended purpose clearly to support classification decision

dimensions.name: CE Marking & MDR Conformity
dimensions.description: If the app is a medical device, does it have the required CE marking?
reflection_questions: Have you initiated the CE marking process for your app?
Do you have a notified body engaged for conformity assessment (if Class IIa+)?
Is your technical documentation complete and up to date?
example_risks: App marketed in the EU without required CE marking
Technical documentation does not meet MDR Annex II requirements
example_mitigations: Engage a notified body early in the development process
Use MDR Annex II checklist to structure technical documentation

dimensions.name: EU AI Act Risk Classification
dimensions.description: If the app uses AI, is it classified correctly under the EU AI Act?
reflection_questions: Does your app contain an AI system as defined by the EU AI Act?
If your app is a medical device with AI, it is likely high-risk — have you planned for compliance?
Are you tracking the EU AI Act implementation timeline (full application by Aug 2027)?
example_risks: AI component not identified, leading to non-compliance when obligations apply
High-risk AI system deployed without required conformity assessment
example_mitigations: Map all AI components and assess their risk classification
Begin compliance preparation now to meet 2027 deadline

dimensions.name: GDPR Compliance (DPO, DPIA)
dimensions.description: Is the app fully compliant with GDPR requirements for health data?
reflection_questions: Have you appointed a Data Protection Officer (DPO)?
Have you conducted a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
Do you have a lawful basis for processing health data under GDPR Art. 9?
example_risks: Processing health data without DPIA
No DPO appointed despite large-scale health data processing
example_mitigations: Conduct DPIA before app launch
Appoint DPO and establish data protection governance structure

dimensions.name: Post-Market Surveillance & Vigilance
dimensions.description: Is there a system to monitor the app's safety and performance after launch?
reflection_questions: Do you have a post-market surveillance plan?
How do you collect and analyze adverse event reports from users?
Is there a process for reporting serious incidents to competent authorities?
example_risks: No mechanism to detect safety issues after deployment
Adverse events reported by users but not escalated to regulators
example_mitigations: Implement in-app adverse event reporting
Establish vigilance procedures aligned with MDR Article 87

dimensions.name: Third-Party Audit & Certification
dimensions.description: Has the app been independently audited or certified?
reflection_questions: Has your app undergone independent security auditing?
Have you pursued any voluntary certifications (ISO 27001, ISO 82304-2)?
Is your app listed on any national health app assessment programs?
example_risks: No independent verification of safety and security claims
Self-certification without external validation
example_mitigations: Commission independent security and clinical safety audits
Apply for national health app library listing (e.g., NHS Apps Library, DiGA)

dimensions.name: Lifecycle & Documentation Management
dimensions.description: Is the app's entire lifecycle documented and governed?
reflection_questions: Do you maintain version-controlled documentation of all design decisions?
Is there a change management process for updates that affect clinical functionality?
How long will you maintain and support the app?
example_risks: No documentation of why clinical thresholds were chosen
App abandoned by developer while patients still depend on it
example_mitigations: Implement quality management system (e.g., ISO 13485)
Define and communicate end-of-life policy to users
